main.text: [II, 533] Chapter 2.
On the dove's feathers, neck, eyes, moaning and flight.

I am pleased to begin the description of the dove with its plumage and feathers, whose beauty [col. 9] the sacred poet commends thus, Psal. LXVIII, 14.: The wings of the dove covered with silver, and its feathers with the paleness of gold. Wings and feathers stand here by συνεκδοχὴν [synekdochēn] for the whole body. Covered with silver, that is, supremely white like silver, and bright with a certain splendour. For silver is called in Greek ἀργύριον [argyrion], from τὸ ἀργὸν, τὸ λευκόν [to argon, to leukon, "the bright, the white"]; and things that are most brilliantly white are called silver. Hence in the poets ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], that is, λευκόπους [leukopous]. So it is in Hesychius, who likewise explains ἀργυροδίνην κρήνην [argyrodinēn krēnēn] as λευκὰ ῥεύματα ἔχουσαν [leuka rheumata echousan]; and in the eighth book of the Aeneid,
— — — — the silver goose,
is, on the testimony of Servius, an epithet of colour. The raven too was once a silver bird, when it equalled doves in whiteness. Ovid, Metam. book 2, Fable 7:

For this was once a silver bird with snowy feathers, so that it equalled doves wholly without blemish. [II, 534] For among doves some are extremely white ^{(1)}. Varro, On Agriculture book 3, ch. 7: The other kind of doves is the tamer, which, content with household food, is usually fed within the threshold of the door. This kind is mostly white in colour. That is, at some times and in some places, not always nor everywhere. For in Greece white doves were seen late, namely when the forces of Xerxes were routed at Mount Athos. This is expressly reported in the Persica by Charon of Lampsacus, who lived at that time and wrote before Herodotus. Athenaeus, book 9: Χάρων δ᾽ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς, ἐν τοῖς Περσικοῖς περὶ Μαρδονίου ἱστορῶν, καὶ τοῦ διαφθαρέντος στρατοῦ Περσικοῦ περὶ τὸν Ἄθω, γράφει ταῦτα· „Καὶ λευκαὶ περιστεραὶ τότε πρῶτον εἰς „Ἕλληνας ἐφάνησαν, πρότερον οὐ γιγνόμεναι“ [Charōn d᾽ ho Lampsakēnos, en tois Persikois peri Mardoniou historōn, kai tou diaphtharentos stratou Persikou peri ton Athō, graphei tauta: "Kai leukai peristerai tote prōton eis Hellēnas ephanēsan, proteron ou gignomenai"]. Charon of Lampsacus, in the Persica, treating of Mardonius and of the Persian army routed at Mount Athos, writes this: "And white doves were then first seen among the Greeks, there having been none before", namely in Greece, not anywhere, as the translator there wrongly has it. Aelian in the Varia book 1, ch. 15: Χάρων δὲ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς περὶ τὸν Ἄθω φανῆναι περιστερὰς λευκὰς λέγει, ὅτε ἐνταῦθα ἀπώλοντο αἱ τῶν Περσῶν τριέρεις παρακάμπτουσαι τὸν Ἄθω [Charōn de ho Lampsakēnos peri ton Athō phanēnai peristeras leukas legei, hote entautha apōlonto hai tōn Persōn triereis parakamptousai ton Athō]; But Charon of Lampsacus asserts that white doves were seen around Athos when the triremes of the Persians perished there while sailing past Athos. There follows in the Psalm ואברותיה בירקרק חרוץ, And its feathers with the paleness of gold; supply covered, which must be repeated from the preceding hemistich. Paleness of gold, that is, gold of paleness, or pale gold. Similar is Habac. II, 6. עב טיט, thickness of mud, for mud of thickness, or thick mud. התואר במקום המתואר, the predicate for the subject, as Kimchi has it here. Gold is called חרוץ charuts, that is, dug out of the earth, here and in Zach. IX, 3. and frequently in Solomon's Proverbs ^{(2)}. From this comes the Greek χρυσός [chrysos]. And the paleness of gold is ירקרק, with doubled letters, so that the meaning is intensified. Accordingly from this very word comes the Ethiopic ወርቅ፡ vvark for gold. The Greek translators rightly call the paleness of gold χλωρότητα χρυσίου [chlōrotēta chrysiou]. For this is the true colour of gold. Hence Diogenes, asked Διὰ τί τὸ χρυσίον χλωρόν ἐστιν; [Dia ti to chrysion chlōron estin?] Why [II, 535] is gold pale?, answered Ὅτι πολλοὺς ἔχει τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας [Hoti pollous echei tous epibouleuontas], Because it has many plotting against it. So it is in Laertius; and Catullus in the wedding of Peleus and Thetis,
O how often she grew paler than the sallow hue of gold!
And again, to Juventius, [col. 10]
A guest paler than a gilded statue.
And Statius to Maximus Junius in the fourth book of the Silvae,
When will the Dalmatian mountains send you back to sweet Latium, where, having seen Dis, the pale miner returns, of the same colour as the gold he has dug up?

And Lucian in the Cock, to a greedy rich man: Οἴμωζε, καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖ, καὶ ὅμοιος γίγνου τὸ χρῶμα τῷ χρυσῷ, προσετηκὼς αὐτῷ [oimōze, kai agrypnei, kai homoios gignou to chrōma tō chrysō, prosetēkōs autō]; Lament and keep watch, and, wasting away over your gold, become like it in colour. Now, if you ask why this golden colour is attributed to doves, Kimchi answers: שיש בכנפי היונה נוצה שהמצהבת כזהב, In the wings of doves there is plumage yellow like gold: namely in the wings of the younger birds, after they have left the nest. The Talmudists observe the same of turtledoves, and say that from this one learns when they are fit or unfit for sacrifice. For since the Law commands that of doves only the young, and of turtledoves only the adults, be offered, they hold that the former become unfit for sacrifice, and the latter fit, precisely when the feathers begin to turn yellow like gold. The words are in the tractate Cholin, chapter 1, folio 22b: מאימתי התורים כשרים משיצהיבו מאימתי בני יונה פסולים משיצהיבו When are turtledoves (for offering) fit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. When are young doves (for offering) unfit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. And on the word משיצהיבו the Gloss has: שיהא כנפי גופן גדולים ואדומים ומזהיבים כזהב, because the feathers of the body become large and red, and yellow like gold. And somewhat earlier: תחילה הציהב כשמתחילין לצהב כנפים שמסביבות צוארן The beginning of the yellowing is when the feathers they have around the neck begin to turn yellow like gold. So also Maimonides in Issure Mizbeach ch. 3, §2: והתורים כשרים משיזהבו Turtledoves are fit for offering from the time they have a golden colour. Where the Gloss is the same as in the Talmud above. But the necks of doves too, when facing the sun, shine with a golden colour. The Philosopher, in the book On Colours: Οἱ τῶν περιστερῶν τράχηλοι, καὶ τῶν ὑδάτων οἱ σταλαγμοὶ φαίνονται χρυσοειδεῖς, τοῦ φωτὸς ἀνακλωμένου [Hoi tōn peristerōn trachēloi, kai tōn hydatōn hoi stalagmoi phainontai chrysoeideis, tou phōtos anaklōmenou]. The necks of doves and drops of water appear to be of a golden colour when the light is reflected. Others write only that they gleam with various colours. Lucretius, book 2, line 800:

As the plumage of doves appears in the sun, which, set about the nape, crowns the neck: [II, 536] for at times it comes to be red with bright fire-bronze, at times, by a certain way of seeing, it seems to mingle green emeralds with sky-blue.

Philo, in the book On Drunkenness: Τὸν αὐχένα τῆς περιστερᾶς ἐν ἡλιακαῖς αὐγαῖς οὐ κατενόησας μυρίας χρωμάτων ἀλλάττοντα ἰδέας; ἢ οὐχὶ φοινικοῦν, καὶ κυανοῦν, πυροπόν τε, καὶ ἀνθρακοειδὲς, ἔτι τε ὠχρὸν, καὶ ἐρυθρὸν, καὶ ἄλλα παντόδαπα ἴσχει χρώματα, ὧν οὐδὲ τὰς κλήσεις ῥάδιον ἀπομνημονεῦσαι [Ton auchena tēs peristeras en hēliakais augais ou katenoēsas myrias chrōmatōn allattonta ideas? ē ouchi phoinikoun, kai kyanoun, pyropon te, kai anthrakoeides, eti te ōchron, kai erythron, kai alla pantodapa ischei chrōmata, hōn oude tas klēseis rhadion apomnēmoneusai]. Have you never seen a dove's neck in the sun's rays varied into countless colours? Does it not have crimson, and sky-blue, and the colours of fire-bronze and of carbuncle, and pale, and red, and colours of every other kind, whose mere names it would not be easy to recount? This Eustathius copied almost word for word in the Hexaemeron, page 29. Nero, in Seneca, Natural Questions book 1, ch. 5:
The necks of Cytherea's dove shine as it moves.

Pliny, book 10, chapter 26: Doves have a certain sense even of glory. You would think they know their own colours and the ordered variety of them. And book 37, chapter 5: The Carchedonian, etc. uncertain in colour, and like the feathers of the green in peacocks' tails and on the necks of doves. Ausonius, on ducks, Epistle 3:
Whom iridescent plumage has painted with varied colour, rivals of doves in their necks.

But these colours are only apparent. Thus in Martianus, book 2, [col. 11] Arcesilas, gazing at the neck of doves and moved by this uncertainty of variation, began to build up further his doctrine of ἀκαταληψία [akatalēpsia]. And Carneades, to prove that our senses are uncertain, brought forward the necks of doves, which change colour at every turn. So Jerome attests in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem. But Oppian, in book 1 of the Cynegetica, taught that the young even in the egg can be marked with various colours, and real ones at that: namely if, when the females are about to mate, there are set before them

— — — — — δαίδαλα πολλὰ Εἵματα πορφύρεα· ταὶ δὲ κλιδὸν ὄσσε βαλοῦσαι, Θυμὸν ἰαινόμεναι τίκτουσ᾽ ἁλιπόρφυρα τέκνα, [— — — — — daidala polla heimata porphyrea; tai de klidon osse balousai, thymon iainomenai tiktous' haliporphyra tekna,]

many richly wrought purple garments: and they, casting sidelong glances at them and delighted in mind, bring forth purple young. I cite this the more gladly because by a similar art Jacob obtained parti-coloured sheep for himself.

The eyes of doves are attributed to the bride in Cant. I, 15. and IV, 1., and to the bridegroom as well in Cant. V, 12.; that is, eyes that are pure, lovely, simple, and finally chaste. This last is what the Hebrews chiefly understand here, because the dove looks only to its mate and does not [II, 537] cast its eyes on any other. Rabbi Selomo: משמכרת את בן זוגה אונה מניחתו שיזדווג לאחר, After she has been betrothed to her mate, she does not delight in being joined to another. And Aben Ezra: מנהג בני יונה שלא להתחבר אלא עם זוגה שלה, Doves are not accustomed to associate with any other than their own mate. Aelian teaches the same of the wood pigeon in Hist. book 3, ch. 44, and then says: Ἐὰν δὲ ἐποφθαλμιάσωσιν ἑτέροις, περιέρχονται αὐτοὺς οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ τὸν μὲν ἄῤῥενα οἱ ὁμογενεῖς διασπῶσιν, αἱ θήλειαι δὲ τὸν θῆλυν [Ean de epophthalmiasōsin heterois, perierchontai autous hoi loipoi, kai ton men arrena hoi homogeneis diaspōsin, hai thēleiai de ton thēlyn]; But if they cast lustful eyes on others, the rest surround them, and the males tear the male to pieces, the females the female. Note here that the verb ἐποφθαλμιᾶν [epophthalmian] is used of a lustful look, because the eyes are the leaders in love, and ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾷν γίνεται ἐρᾷν [ek tou horan ginetai eran]. Hence John ^{a)} speaks of Ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν [Hē epithymia tōn ophthalmōn], and Peter ^{b)} of ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες μεστοὺς μοιχαλίδος [ophthalmous echontes mestous moichalidos]. David ^{c)}, having learned this to his own cost, earnestly asked God to turn his eyes away so that they should not behold vanity. And Job ^{d)} made a covenant with them that they should not look upon a virgin. The interpreters inquire anxiously what these words refer to in Cant. V, 12.: His eyes (the bridegroom's) are like (the eyes) of doves by the streams of waters, washed in milk, dwelling by the fullness. I think the sacred writer had only this in view: that doves have livelier eyes by the waters, because they prefer to live near them. Accordingly Varro (De re rustica, book 3, chapter 7), in his description of the dovecote, τῆς περιστεροφείου [tēs peristeropheiou], says: There should be pure water flowing in, from which they can both drink and bathe; for these birds are very clean. And they are described not only as by the waters but also as by the fullness (supply "of the waters", as Scripture repeatedly speaks ^{e)} of the fullness of the sea), that is, by places where waters gush forth and come up close to the top of the banks, so that they are easy to drink from. The same doves are said to be washed in milk, that is, very white, as if things washed in milk became white, as things washed in ink become black. Compare Job. IX, 30.: If I wash myself with snow water, and cleanse my hands with soap. Far-fetched, and found nowhere else so far as I know, is the view of Gregory on the Canticle, chapter 5, that doves sit beside streams so that they may see in the water the shadow of birds flying overhead, and by throwing themselves upon it may thus escape the talons of birds of prey. But this seems to have been taken in part from the story of a certain bird which in Arabic is called خاطف ظله [khāṭif ẓillihi] chatipho-dhillihi, as if to say snatcher of its own shadow, because اذا راي ظله في الما اقبل اليه ليخطفه [idhā rāy ẓillahu fī al-mā aqbala ilayhi li-yakhṭafahu], when it sees its shadow in the water, it approaches it in order to snatch it. So Alcamus. In Damir it is called otherwise: [col. 12] قرلا [qirlā] koralla, a Persian word; رفراف [rafrāf] riphraph, from the fluttering of its wings; and [II, 538] ملاعب ظله [mulāʿib ẓillihi] mulaibo dhillihi, playing with its shadow. It is asserted to be في جنس العصافير [fī jins al-ʿaṣāfīr] of the kind of sparrows, or small birds. It is therefore not the jackdaw, which I once thought it was, because Tzetzes says of jackdaws in Chiliad 4, Hist. 119:

— εἴπερ χέεις ἔλαιον ἔν τινι λεκανίσκῃ, Πρὸς τὴν σκιὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν τοὺς κολοιοὺς κρατήσῃς. Ναρκίσσους ἄλλους Λάκωνας ὄντας τῶν φιλοσκίων. [— eiper cheeis elaion en tini lekaniskē, Pros tēn skian tēn heautōn tous koloious kratēsēs. Narkissous allous Lakōnas ontas tōn philoskiōn.]

If you pour oil into a small basin, you will hold the jackdaws fast at their own shadow, as if they were Laconian Narcissi, of those who love their own shadow. Note in passing that Narcissus was not a Laconian but a Boeotian, as Ovid, Metam. book 3, Fab. 5, Conon, Hist. 24, Strabo, book 9, Hyginus, Fab. 271, Pausanias in the Boeotica, Claudian, book 2 de raptu, and countless others attest. Yet Tzetzes makes him a Laconian both here and in Chil. 1, Hist. 9, as if he were a countryman of Hyacinthus, with whom he compares him in Hist. 11. This μνημονικὸν σφάλμα [mnēmonikon sphalma] is not to be tolerated in a man who, in that very passage, boasts thus:
Οὐδὲ γὰρ μνημονέστερον τοῦ Τζέτζου Θεὸς ἄλλον Ἄνδρα τῶν πρίν τε, καὶ τῶν νῦν ἐξέφηνεν ἐν βίῳ. [Oude gar mnēmonesteron tou Tzetzou Theos allon Andra tōn prin te, kai tōn nyn exephēnen en biō.]

For God has not brought into life any other man more mindful than Tzetzes, of those who have been or who now are. And shortly before he had said that he knew all books. But, to return to the point from which we digressed, the Hebrews render the sacred words, which we refer to doves as to the eyes of doves, thus: His eyes are like doves' (eyes) by the courses of waters, washed with milk, set in fullness, that is, filling their place like a gem its setting. This is what in Hebrew is called מלואת אבן, fullness or filling of stone, Exod. XXVIII, 17. So Aben Ezra and R. Selomo, who holds that the eyes are described as לא בולטות יותר מדאי ולא שיקעות אלא יושבות מלאת גומא שלהם, neither more prominent than is fitting, nor sunken, but so placed that they fill their socket. And the recent interpreters follow this. But in this interpretation I find some things lacking. First, that in this way a milky colour seems to be attributed to the eyes, whose principal part, that is, the pupil, is black, or blue, etc. Second, that although stones enclosed in a setting are called in Hebrew אבני מלואים, stones of fillings, that is, which fill the setting, and the setting of a stone in a bezel is called מלואת אבן, filling of stone, yet a stone set in a bezel is nowhere said to be יושב על מלאת, remaining at fullness. Nor indeed can this be said. For who would say that money remains or stands at the fullness of a bag, or wine at the fullness of a cask, when the bag is full of money, or the cask full of wine ^{(3)}?
[II, 539] In the voice of the dove there is something plaintive and moaning. Hence doves are said to moan. The author of the Philomela:
And the chaste turtledove and the dove moan.
Virgil, Eclogue 1: Yet meanwhile neither will the hoarse wood-pigeons, your care, nor the turtledove cease to moan from the airy elm.
Martial, book 3, Epigr. 57:
Here moans the wood-pigeon, there the wax-coloured turtledove.

Gregory on Job, book 32, ch. 4: We know that the young of doves, or turtledoves, have moaning instead of song. And on the Song, ch. 1: The dove in its love moans instead of singing. For the Greeks too this same thing is στένειν [stenein]. Theocritus, Idyll 7, verse 141:
Ἄειδον κόρυδοι, καὶ ἀκανθίδες, ἔστενε τρυγὼν, [Aeidon korydoi, kai akanthides, estene trygōn,]

The larks and goldfinches were singing, the turtledove was moaning. Hence Chrysostom, in the Homily On the Turtledove: Ἡ τρυγὼν ἡ φιλέρημος, ὅτε ἐν ὕλαις συγκοιταζομένη καλεῖ τὸν ὁμόζυγον, γοεραῖς κολακείαις τὰς κοιλάδας δονήσασα· [Hē trygōn hē philerēmos, hote en hylais synkoitazomenē kalei ton homozygon, goerais kolakeiais tas koilada donēsasa;] The solitary turtledove, when lying in the woods it calls its mate, stirring the valleys with mournful blandishments. [col. 13] Others say that turtledoves τρύζειν [tryzein] and doves γογγύζειν [gongyzein]. Pollux, book 5, chapter 13, §. 2, which is entitled Ὄρνεων φωναὶ [Orneōn phōnai], Voices of Birds: Εἴποις ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν [Eipois an trygonas tryzein, peristeras gongyzein]. Γογγύζειν [Gongyzein] means to murmur. Hence you may find murmura [murmurs] for the moaning of doves: as when the emperor Gallienus, in Trebellius, says of the bride and groom in an epithalamium,
— — — let not doves surpass your murmurs, nor ivy your arms, nor shells your kisses.

But the Hebrew has הגה, which is rightly rendered by the verb to moan, since it everywhere refers to mourning. So in the song of King Hezekiah about his illness, Es. XXXVIII,14. [II, 540] אהגה כיונה, I moaned like a dove. And Es. LIX, 11., where the afflicted condition of the Jews is treated: We all growl like bears, וכיונים הגה נהגה, and like doves we moan with moaning, that is, with heavy and continuous moaning ^{(4)}. But המה too, which properly means to roar, applies to the moaning of doves, when it is said in Ezech. VII, 16. כיוני הגאות כלם הומות איש בעונו, like doves of the valleys they all roared (that is, moaned), each for his own sin. For כיוני הגיאות, like doves of the valleys, the Septuagint read כיונה הגות. Hence arose that rendering ὡς περιστεραὶ μελετητικαὶ [hōs peristerai meletētikai], like moaning doves. For with them μελετᾷν [meletan], said of doves, means to moan. Accordingly Theodoret on this passage: Ὀδυρόμενοι γὰρ καὶ θρηνοῦντες περιστεραῖς μελετώσαις ἀπεικαθήσονται· στένουσι γὰρ ἔοικε τῶν περιστερῶν ἡ φωνή [Odyromenoi gar kai thrēnountes peristerais meletōsais apeikasthēsontai; stenousi gar eoike tōn peristerōn hē phōnē]. This must certainly be rendered thus: For those who lament and mourn will be compared to moaning doves (not to doves on high, as the translator has it here). For the voice of doves is like that of people moaning. The voice of the dove is also taken for mournful moaning in Nahum II, 7., where the queen of Nineveh, as she is led into captivity, is accompanied by maidservants moaning, as with the voice of doves, and beating their breasts. The Hebrew has מנהגות כקול יונים, leading away as with the voice of doves. Leading away here, as they hold, is the same as accompanying, and moaning must be supplied. For to lead away is put for to lead away and to moan: one for two. So in Prov. XXV, 22., You will take coals of fire upon his head, for you will take and put; and Psal. LXVIII, 19., You received gifts for men, for you received and gave, or you received things to give. Accordingly Paul renders it he gave gifts to men, Ephes. IV, 8. What if for מנהגות, leading away, one were to read מהגות, moaning, with one small letter less? The sense would thus be plainer; yet I would not dare to change anything, since it is established that the most ancient translators read מנהגות ^{(5)}.

Scripture praises the flight of the dove more than once. Thus Esa. LX, 8.: Who are these that fly together like clouds, and like doves to their windows? The Rabbis refer this [II, 541] to the Israelites, who were to return from the Babylonian captivity with the greatest eagerness. Hence the Chaldee paraphrast: Who are these who come openly like swift clouds without delay? The exiles of Israel, who are gathered and return to their land, כיונין דתיבין לגו שובכיהן, like doves that return to their dovecotes. On these words Kimchi: יותר יעופו מהרה בשובם אל קניהם ממה שיעופו בצאתם מהם מפני שהם ממהרות לשוב אל גוזליהם שהניחו להאכילם מאשר בפיהם, They fly faster when they return to their nests than when they go out from them, because they hasten to return to the young they have left, to offer them the food which they have in their mouth. A similar passage is Os. XI, 11.: They will tremble like a little bird out of Egypt, and like a dove from the land of Assyria. They will tremble, יחרדו, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. So 1 Sam. XVI, 4., when Samuel came to Bethlehem, ויחרדו, And the elders of the city trembled (that is, hurried in agitation) to meet him. And in this same prophet, Ose. III, 5.: They will tremble to the Lord and to his goodness, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. Aben Ezra: [col. 14] ישובו במהרה במרוצא פתע פתאום, They will return hastily, at a run, quickly, swiftly. Yet in the sacred text there is not חרדו but its synonym פחדו. Indeed, verbs of trembling sometimes relate to haste. Virgil, in the ninth book of the Aeneid:
Do not tremble, Teucrians, to defend my ships.

that is, do not hurry. So Servius and Nonius Marcellus. And Livy, book 23: And soon, while each hurries [trepidat] running about to his own duties at the first signals. Trepidat, that is, festinat [hurries]. So certainly in Hosea: They will tremble like a dove (that is, they will flee with the utmost haste) from Assyria ^{(6)}. For the flight of the dove is extremely swift. Hence it is that in Psal. LV, 7. David wishes for the wings of a dove, to withdraw by swift flight from imminent danger. Who (he says) will give me a wing like a dove's, with which I might fly away to safety? Behold, I would wander as far away as possible, to stay in the wilderness. And I would hasten my escape, swifter than the most rapid wind and whirlwind. Just as the Chorus in Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus:

Εἴτ᾽, ἀελλαία ταχύῤ- [Eit', aellaia tachyr-] Would that, like a dove of swift ῥωστος πελειὰς, [rhōstos peleias,] whirlwind onrush, Αἰθερίας νεφέλας [Aitherias nephelas] I might pass through Κύρσαί με, [Kyrsai me,] etc. the ethereal clouds, etc.

Gregory of Nazianzus, in Oration 17, says that David longed for the wings of a dove ὡς κουφοτέρας, καὶ ταχυτέρας [hōs kouphoteras, kai tachyteras], as being lighter and swifter. And Jansenius in his Paraphrase: O that wings were given me such as the dove has, which of all birds is the swiftest in flight; so that, as by its most rapid flight, and by that alone, it frees itself from [II, 542] its enemy the hawk, etc. Pliny too, book 10, chapter 36, says that doves in free flight are much swifter than the hawk. And Phaedrus, book 1, Fable 31:
The doves, when they had often fled the kite, And by the swiftness of their wings escaped death.
And Euripides, of the Bacchae hastening to the slaughter of Pentheus:
Ἤιξαν πελέιας ὠκύτητ᾽ οὐκ ἥσσονες, [Ēixan peleias ōkytēt᾽ ouk hēssones,]
They rushed on, not inferior to doves in swiftness. Accordingly Virgil, Aeneid book 5, compares the ship of Mnestheus, which
With the swift stroke of oars, and the winds called up, Makes for the sloping seas, and runs down the open main,
to a dove in flight, at the moment when
It is borne flying into the fields, and gliding through the still air Skims its liquid path, and does not move its swift wings.

And, so that the Argo may be believed to have been a very swift ship, the poets describe it as quick ὅσον πελειάδος [hoson peleiados], like a dove. And they invent the story that a dove was sent by the Argonauts between the Symplegades, and that when it had got through, they concluded from this that the Argo too would get through, as Eustathius teaches on Odyssey μ´. The Arabs and Hebrews agree with this. Thus Damir, after teaching that الشهرمان والشاهين [al-shahramān wa-l-shāhīn], the saharman and the sahin, species of hawk, are most hostile to the dove, says: وهو اطير منهما ومن ساير الطير كلها [wa-huwa aṭyar minhumā wa-min sāyir al-ṭayr kullihā] And it surpasses them in flight, and all birds whatsoever. And on the passage of the Psalm that we have cited, R. Simon, R. Iodan, R. Jonah, and R. Kimchi, to the question why David prefers the wings of the dove to the wings of other birds, answer thus: כל העופות בשעה שיגעים הם נסים על גבי הסלע או על גבי האילן ונתפסין אבל יונה בשעה שיגעה היא קובצת אחת מאגפיה ופורחת באחת והיא נצולת ואינה נתפסת, All other birds, when they are tired from flying, flee onto a rock or onto a tree, and are caught; but the dove, when it is tired, folds one of its wings and flies with the other, and so escapes and is not caught. And Aben Ezra: והזכיר יונה [col. 15] שהיא עם בני אדם ועמה ישגרו המלכים ספריהם, He mentions the dove because it lives with men, and kings send letters by it. Indeed, in the twelfth century after Christ, when Aben Ezra wrote, this was much practised. Paulus Aemilius, On the Deeds of the Franks, book 4, where he speaks of the governor of Hasarchum, a town of Syria: His envoys (sent to Baldwin to beg for help) tied a letter to the tail of a dove which they had brought with them from home when they set out on their embassy, and sent it back as agreed. Thus informed, the governor defended himself excellently [II, 543]. And where he speaks of Jerusalem besieged by the Christians: It happened that a dove flying over the camp of the Latins, descending as a hawk pressed upon it, was caught by our men. Under its wings was found a letter written in Arabic, both in words and in letters. And in book 5: While they were encamped before the walls (of Tyre), some authors say that a dove flew up. When our men, taught by experience, recognized it as a letter-carrier, so great a shout was raised by the land and naval forces of the Latins that the bird, as if driven by a whirlwind of the disturbed air, fell to the ground. The letter taken from it, written in barbarian characters to the Tyrians, said that help would soon come, that they should be of good courage and endure the siege a few days. Our men, on the other hand, had another letter written in the hand and language of those barbarians whom they held in their power etc. and sent the bird back with the forged and deceitful letter, telling the besieged to take counsel for themselves according to their present need, etc. that no hope of help near at hand could be held out, etc. The Tyrians yielded to the trick. Marmol, in his Africa, book 2, chapter 31, refers this to the year 1123. On the same matter see Jacques de Vitry, Histor. Orient. book 1; Arnold of Lübeck in the History of the Slavs; Vincent in the Doctrinale book 16, ch. 154; and Wildebrand of Oldenburg in the Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum, where he wrongly ascribes to the people of Tripoli what others attribute to the Tyrians. But older histories too offer us examples of the same art. For, to pass over fables, such as what the Samaritans write in chapter 20 of their spurious book of Joshua, that after defeating the five kings he informed Eleazar of this victory by a letter tied to the wings of birds, and in chapter 34 that he sent a letter to Nebichus by the service of a dove; and what we read in Aelian, History, book 6, chapter 7, that Mares, king of Egypt, used a crow to carry letters wherever he wished: to pass over these, I say, since they are plainly fabulous, why should we not believe what is found in Aelian's Varia, book 9, chapter 2, that Taurosthenes, the Ὀλυμπιονίκην [Olympionikēn], announced his victory to his father in Aegina from Olympia on the same day by a dove as messenger? They say, namely, περιστερὰν τὸν Ταυροσθένην ἐπάγεσθαι ἀπολιποῦσαν τοὺς ἑαυτῆς νεοσσοὺς ὑγροὺς ἔτι, καὶ ἀπτῆνας, νικήσαντα, καὶ ἀφεῖναι τὴν πελειάδα, προσάψαντα πορφύραν αὐτῇ· τὴν δὲ ἐπειγομένην πρὸς τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ἀπαυθημερῆσαι ἐκ Πίσσης εἰς Αἴγιναν· [peristeran ton Taurosthenēn epagesthai apolipousan tous heautēs neossous hygrous eti, kai aptēnas, nikēsanta, kai apheinai tēn peleiada, prosapsanta porphyran autē; tēn de epeigomenēn pros tous neottous, apauthēmerēsai ek Pissēs eis Aiginan] that Taurosthenes took with him a dove taken away from its chicks, still tender and unfledged; and when he had won, he sent it back with a piece of purple tied to it, and it, hastening with all speed to its chicks, flew on the same day from Pisa to Aegina. Pliny and Frontinus report that something similar happened at the siege of Mutina, although they hardly agree with each other. For the latter, in book 3 of the Stratagems, writes that Hirtius sent letters, tied with a bristle to a dove's neck, to Decimus Brutus, besieged in Mutina by Antony; the former, in book 10, chapter 37, says that doves were messengers in great affairs, with letters attached to their feet, at the siege of Mutina, when D. Brutus sent them to the consuls' camp. But in the same siege [II, 544] the same Brutus could have both received and sent back letters by the service of doves. You may often see the poets allude to this skill of doves. Among them Anacreon, in Ode 9, attributes the following to his dove:

Ἐγὼ δ᾽ Ἀνακρέοντι [Egō d᾽ Anakreonti] And I, for Anacreon, Διακονῶ τοσαῦτα, [Diakonō tosauta,] serve in such matters, Καὶ νῦν οἵας ἐκείνου [Kai nyn hoias ekeinou] And now see [col. 16] Ἐπιστολὰς κομίζω. [Epistolas komizō.] what letters of his I carry.
Pherecrates in the Painters, in Athenaeus, book 9:
Ἀπόπεμψον ἀγγέλλοντα, τὸν περιστερὸν, [Apopempson angellonta, ton peristeron,]
Send back the dove as messenger. Martial, on a dove that flew down into the lap of Aretulla, book 8, Epigram 32:
Perhaps this bird has come to you from the Sardinian shores of the exile, a messenger that your brother will return.
To these I cannot help adding these few lines from the most charming Elegy of the late Heinsius on the doves of Leiden, book 3, Elegy 10:

Here he sends the sacred bird down from the anxious city, to carry back his directions; she flies. And soon, rejoicing to see her home and sweet nest again, she glided back through the midst of the air. She carries in her wings the letters and orders of Boisot, and has now completed the sweet work of her service.

This art, which had nearly died out in our fathers' time, the Dutch revived. So too did the Turks: Linschoten, in his description of Ormuz, chapter 6, writes that their emperor learns within a short time by means of doves what is happening in the most remote parts of his empire. Accordingly, in the book On Animals, which Calonymus translated from the Arabic of Abulsaphe into Hebrew in the year of Christ 1316, it is said of the dove: היונה המסולסל הוא זה המגביה לעוף נושה כתבים ואגרות מארץ אל ארץ לחבונתו, The dove, raising itself on high, that is, which is exalted in its flight, when by its intelligence it carries letters from place to place. For, as Alkazuinius says, اذا ارسل من موضع بعيد يصعد نحو الهوا وتكون صعوده مدورا فلا يزال يصعد وينظر حتي يري شيا من علامات بلده فعند ذلك يهبط اليها بادني زمان [idhā ursila min mawḍiʿ baʿīd yaṣʿad naḥwa al-hawā wa-takūn ṣuʿūduhu mudawwaran fa-lā yazāl yaṣʿad wa-yanẓur ḥattī yarī shayan min ʿalāmāt baladihi fa-ʿinda dhālika yahbiṭ ilayhā bi-adnā zamān] When it is sent from a very distant place, it climbs into the highest air, and its ascent is made in a circle. Nor does it stop climbing and looking about until it notices some sign of its own region. Then it descends to it [II, 545] in a short time. And Damir: في طبعه انه يطلب وكره ولو ارسل من الف فرسخ ويحمل الاخبار وياتي بها من المسافة البعيدة في المده القريبة وفيه ما يقطع ثلاثة الاف فرسخ في يوم واحد [fī ṭabʿihi annahu yaṭlub wakrahu wa-law ursila min alf farsakh wa-yaḥmil al-akhbār wa-yātī bihā min al-masāfa al-baʿīda fī al-mudda al-qarība wa-fīhi mā yaqṭaʿ thalāthat ālāf farsakh fī yawm wāḥid] And its nature is to seek its nest again, even if it is sent from a thousand parasangs, and to carry messages from the most remote places in the shortest time, so that some are said to have covered three thousand parasangs in a single day. This exceeds all belief, and I think it was invented by those who tell of great things as still greater. The little letter that is tied to the dove is called in Arabic by a special name, بطاقة [biṭāqa] bittaka, that is, πιττάκιον [pittakion], pittacium [slip]. And زجل [zajala] zagiala means to send out a dove for this purpose; and a dove so sent is called زجال [zijāl] zigial. So it is in Alcamus ^{(7)}.

The same author has this on the dove of Palestine, p. 553: “The size of a wood pigeon. The neck, head, breast and shoulders are grey. The back grey with dark spots. The tail feathers and flight feathers white at the tip. The eyes and feet are reddish.”

But Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. III, p. 950, note, rightly pointed out that this etymology is far too broad, since absolutely all metals are dug out of the earth. He nevertheless omitted what A. Schultens discussed concerning this word in Commentar. ad Prov. XXI, 5, p. 252. Gold seems to have been called חרוץ because in some places of Arabia Felix, where rain pours heavily over ground rich in gold, the gold is laid bare and so is found as if already dug out, not by art but of its own accord. See the passage from Taurizius, the grammarian, cited by Schultens in the place mentioned.
1 Par. XVI, 32. Ps. XCVI, 11. et XCVIII, 7. etc.

The ancient interpreters also understood the word מלאת, with unanimous agreement, of the fullness of waters, as Bochart explained above. See HUFNAGEL's [II, 539] Observationes in Canticum Canticorum (under the title Auch etwas übers hohe Lied) in the Repertorium für bibl. und morgenl. Litterat. edited by Eichhorn, vol. XI, p. 131. Moreover, what Bochart remarks here about the interpretation of the word מלאת devised by some of the Hebrews applies also to Velthusen, who in his commentary on this passage (Der Schwesternhandel, eine morgenländische Idyllenkette, mit historischkritischen Untersuchungen pp. 425–428) brings forward much from his manifold store of learning to explain the simile used by the Hebrew poet, but little, I suspect, that bears on the matter. By doves washed in milk our poet undoubtedly meant to express the pure and, as it were, radiant whiteness of the eyes around the pupils. That these doves are pictured as sitting by the waters belongs to the ornament of the image; no further simile should be sought in this. It is tedious to report the guesses of other interpreters.

The original sense of the verb הגה, which lies in seething heat, and the series of meanings derived from it, since it is then transferred to all the more agitated and vehement emotions, whether these seethe inwardly in the mind (hence it is also used of meditation, which for an Oriental is a kind of agitation and commotion of the mind) or boil over and burst out into murmurs, moaning, howls, cries (hence also of the roaring of a lion), and into songs, both mournful and satirical: all this ALB. Schultens uncovered and expounded with the help of the Arabic هجى [hajā] in his Commentarius in Prov. p. 320 ff., compare p. 71; further in his Commentar. in Iob. p. 1040, and in the Animadverss. Philologg. in Thren. Ierem. Chapter III, v. 62, p. 509.

But everything is plain, and there is no need either to supply some verb or to alter the received reading, if the verb נהג is explained from the Arabic نهج [nahaja] to sigh, to moan, to draw sighs, as ALB. Schultens first showed in Animadverss. Philoll. ad Nah. II, 7, p. 342; to whom add I. D. Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. V, p. 1603.

Compare ALB. Schultens, Animadverss. Philologg. on Esaj. XIX. 17., p. 265 of the Opera minora, Leiden 1769. ED. Pococke shows a similar use of the Arabic verb فزع [fazaʿa] in his Commentar. on Hos. III, 5.

On carrier doves, whose service the Turks still use today for carrying letters, much is reported by DELLA VALLE in his Travels vol. I, letter 12, pp. 128–129 of the German translation (who asserts that a six days' journey is completed by a carrier dove in a single day), and by ALEX. RUSSELL in the Natural History of Aleppo p. 66. The plan of our work does not allow us to transcribe these passages here, since they are too long.
